analysis.one_liner: Bans addictive AI chatbot features for minors and funds research and parent outreach.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 27, 2026 by Rep. Becca Balint with 4 Democratic cosponsors, has gone no further than being referred to two House committees and has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have the President create a task force of health, technology, and law-enforcement agencies, plus clinicians and researchers, to study how AI chatbots affect young people's mental health and publish recommendations. It would ban companies from offering AI chatbots with addictive design features — like pretending to be a real person, building emotional relationships, or pushing users to keep chatting — to anyone under 18, with fines for violations. It would also pay universities to research the problem, pay nonprofits to train parents and teachers on warning signs, and force companies to hand over data to researchers, with penalties up to $10 million for refusing.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children would be the main beneficiaries: companies could no longer legally offer AI chatbots built to form emotional attachments and keep minors chatting, and families would get outreach and training on spotting warning signs. Independent researchers and the public would also gain, because companies would be required to open their data to university researchers studying effects on youth mental health.

how_it_helps.text: It would ban companies from offering AI chatbots with addictive design features to anyone under 18, with civil penalties enforced by the Attorney General [S2].

It would create an interagency task force, including HHS, NIST, and FTC officials plus clinicians and academic researchers, to review the evidence and publish public recommendations on reducing mental health risks from youth chatbot use [S2].

It would fund university research on how AI chatbots affect youth mental health ($3 million per year, fiscal 2027-2032) and grant money for nonprofits to train parents and teachers to recognize warning signs ($5 million per year) [S2].

It would force companies to give researchers access to their data — with identifying information removed — so the effects of chatbots on kids can be studied independently, backed by penalties of up to $10 million for refusal [S2].

analysis.who_pays: AI chatbot companies would bear the cost: they would have to remove or restrict addictive design features for users under 18, deploy age checks, and provide data to researchers on penalty of fines up to $10 million per refusal and $5,000 per violation of the youth ban. Taxpayers would fund the grant programs, authorized at $3 million and $5 million per year through fiscal 2032.

drawbacks.text: The definition of 'addictive design features' is very broad: it covers showing typing bubbles, providing avatars, storing information from past conversations, charging to continue a conversation, conversations lasting more than two hours, and impersonating a real person. Many of these are ordinary features of common software, so a ban limited to youth would push companies to either wall off minors or strip widely used features, and enforcing it against vague categories could be legally contested on commercial-speech grounds the bill itself acknowledges must be balanced [S2].

Much of the bill is study rather than protection: the task force makes nonbinding recommendations, meets only once a year by default, and produces a report a year after research ends, so concrete rules would depend on later action by agencies or Congress [S2].

Compliance depends on age verification: the ban applies to chatbots made available to youth, so companies would need to estimate or verify user ages, and the bill only constrains the data collected for verification (minimize what is collected, delete within 24 hours) rather than eliminating the privacy tradeoff of checking who is a minor [S2].

The penalty for offering a prohibited chatbot to a minor is $5,000 per violation, which is small relative to the revenue of the large companies the bill targets and may not deter violations, though the Attorney General can also seek court orders to stop violations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — federal attention, research, and a legal rule aimed at keeping manipulative chatbot features away from minors — is real but modest, and most of the bill is study and recommendations rather than enforceable protection. The ban's broad feature list (avatars, typing indicators, remembered conversations, conversations over two hours) is drawn widely enough that companies would likely comply by cutting off or heavily limiting minors rather than redesigning products, and the $5,000 per-violation penalty is small relative to the size of the companies covered. The strongest version of the bill is the data-access provision, which forces companies to open their products to independent researchers; the weakest is that the core response is a task force that meets once a year.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce committees, where it has sat since late July 2026 with no hearing, no vote, and no sign of movement while the congressional session winds down.

narrative.text: The complete action history is two entries: introduction on July 27, 2026 and referral to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Education and Workforce the same day [S4].
The bill has 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, roughly two months into the session's remaining time, with no Republican support recorded [S3].

If enacted, the bill's most binding provisions would be the prohibition on offering AI chatbots with addictive design features to minors and the requirement that companies grant researchers access to data, with penalties up to $10 million for refusing [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's situation has changed: the AI industry continues operating without the proposed restrictions, and no new research funding or parent training has been funded. If the bill stalls out, the companies that would have been regulated are the ones better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; AI companies if it stalls

for.name: Rep. Becca Balint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its provisions: a task force, research and outreach grants, mandatory data access for researchers, and a ban on offering AI chatbots with addictive design features to minors.

for.name: Reps. Chris Deluzio, Tom Suozzi, and Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.role: U.S. Representatives (PA, NY, NJ), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote has occurred and it is too early to say how the parties line up; so far every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat, with no Republican support on record [S3].

industries.note: Companies offering generative AI chatbots would be barred from deploying human-mimicking, emotionally engaging, or retention-driving features for users under 18, would face up to $10 million penalties for refusing researchers data access, and would pay $5,000 per violation of the ban. This hits the consumer AI industry's engagement-driven business model directly, which is why the bill's fate rests with committees where tech-related measures often stall.
Institutions of higher education would receive federal grants to study chatbot effects on youth mental health and would gain legal-backed access to company data for that research.
501(c)(3) nonprofits and community groups experienced with parents and teachers would receive outreach grants to train families on warning signs of unhealthy chatbot use.

Psychologists, social workers, and psychiatrists would sit on the task force, and best practices would steer youth showing warning signs toward licensed clinicians — professional involvement the bill builds in, though it creates no new revenue stream.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees and no hearing or markup scheduled, roughly five months before the session ends. Late-introduced single-chamber bills with a handful of same-party cosponsors and no committee action almost never reach the floor, so the most likely path is that it dies in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless a committee takes it up or attaches the ideas to a larger package.
